O: She is still with her dying friend, and is still the same bright, beautiful creature whose presence softens pain, and sheds happiness around whichever way she turns.
She went out yesterday with her little sisters:
I knew it, and went to meet them;
and we walked together.
In about an hour and a half we returned to the town.
We stopped at the spring I am so fond of, and which is now a thousand times dearer to me than ever.
Charlotte seated herself upon the low wall, and we gathered about her.
I looked around, and recalled the time when my heart was unoccupied and free.
"Dear fountain!"
I said, "since that time I have no more come to enjoy cool repose by thy fresh stream:
I have passed thee with careless steps, and scarcely bestowed a glance upon thee."
I looked down, and observed Charlotte's little sister, Jane, coming up the steps with a glass of water.
I turned toward Charlotte, and I felt her influence over me.
Jane at the moment approached with the glass.
Her sister, Marianne, wished to take it from her.
"No!"
cried the child, with the sweetest expression of face, "Charlotte must drink first."
M: She's still with her dying friend, and still the same bright, lovely creature who eases pain and scatters happiness wherever she turns.
Yesterday evening she went walking with her little sisters;
I knew it, met them, and we went on together.
After about an hour and a half we turned back toward town.
We stopped at the spring I love so much — now a thousand times dearer to me than before.
Charlotte sat down on the low wall and we gathered round her.
I looked about me, and the time when my heart was still free and empty came back to me.
"Dear spring," I said, "since then I've never once come to rest by your cool water;
sometimes, hurrying past, I haven't even glanced at you."
I looked down and saw Charlotte's little sister Jane coming up the steps with a glass of water.
I turned to Charlotte, and felt all over again what she is to me.
Just then Jane came up with the glass, and her sister Marianne tried to take it from her.
"No!"
the child cried, with the sweetest look, "no — Charlotte must drink first!"

O: I have paid my visit to my native place with all the devotion of a pilgrim, and have experienced many unexpected emotions.

Near the great elm tree, which is a quarter of a league from the village, I got out of the carriage, and sent it on before, that alone, and on foot, I might enjoy vividly and heartily all the pleasure of my recollections.
I stood there under that same elm which was formerly the term and object of my walks.
How things have since changed!
Then, in happy ignorance, I sighed for a world I did not know, where I hoped to find every pleasure and enjoyment which my heart could desire;
and now, on my return from that wide world, O my friend, how many disappointed hopes and unsuccessful plans have I brought back!
M: I've made the pilgrimage to my birthplace with all a pilgrim's reverence, and many an unlooked-for feeling took hold of me.

By the great linden that stands a quarter-hour from the town on the way to S—, I had the carriage stop, got down, and sent it on, so as to go on foot and taste every memory new and warm and to my heart's content.
There I stood under the linden that was once, when I was a boy, the goal and the boundary of my walks.
How different now!
Then, in happy ignorance, I longed out into the unknown world, where I hoped to find such nourishment, such delight for my heart, to fill and satisfy its stirring, hungry yearning.
Now I come back from that wide world — oh, my friend, with how many shattered hopes, how many ruined plans!

O: I passed the bridge of Pélissier, where the ravine, which the river forms, opened before me, and I began to ascend the mountain that overhangs it.
Soon after, I entered the valley of Chamounix.
This valley is more wonderful and sublime, but not so beautiful and picturesque as that of Servox, through which I had just passed.
The high and snowy mountains were its immediate boundaries, but I saw no more ruined castles and fertile fields.
Immense glaciers approached the road;
I heard the rumbling thunder of the falling avalanche and marked the smoke of its passage.
Mont Blanc, the supreme and magnificent Mont Blanc, raised itself from the surrounding _aiguilles_, and its tremendous _dôme_ overlooked the valley.
M: I crossed the bridge at Pélissier, where the river gorge opened before me, and began ascending the mountain above it.
Soon I entered the valley of Chamounix — more wonderful and sublime than the valley of Servox I'd just passed through, but not as beautiful or picturesque.
The high, snowy mountains formed its immediate boundaries.
I saw no more ruined castles or fertile fields.
Immense glaciers came right to the road.
I heard the rumbling thunder of falling avalanches and saw the smoke of their passage.
Mont Blanc — supreme and magnificent — rose from the surrounding peaks, its tremendous dome overlooking the valley.

O: You have read this strange and terrific story, Margaret;
and do you not feel your blood congeal with horror, like that which even now curdles mine?
Sometimes, seized with sudden agony, he could not continue his tale;
at others, his voice broken, yet piercing, uttered with difficulty the words so replete with anguish.
His fine and lovely eyes were now lighted up with indignation, now subdued to downcast sorrow and quenched in infinite wretchedness.
Sometimes he commanded his countenance and tones and related the most horrible incidents with a tranquil voice, suppressing every mark of agitation;
then, like a volcano bursting forth, his face would suddenly change to an expression of the wildest rage as he shrieked out imprecations on his persecutor.
M: You've read this strange and terrifying story, Margaret.
Doesn't your blood run cold with horror, as mine does even now?
Sometimes, seized by sudden agony, he couldn't continue.
Other times his voice — broken but piercing — forced out words drenched in anguish.
His fine eyes would blaze with outrage, then sink into sorrowful despair, then go dark with infinite wretchedness.
Sometimes he controlled his expression and tone, relating the most horrible events in a calm voice, suppressing every sign of agitation.
Then, like a volcano erupting, his face would twist into the wildest rage as he screamed curses at his tormentor.

O: “If I am so scared now, what would it be if it somehow came to pass that I were really going to do it?”
he could not help asking himself as he reached the fourth storey.
There his progress was barred by some porters who were engaged in moving furniture out of a flat.
He knew that the flat had been occupied by a German clerk in the civil service, and his family.
This German was moving out then, and so the fourth floor on this staircase would be untenanted except by the old woman.
“That’s a good thing anyway,” he thought to himself, as he rang the bell of the old woman’s flat.
The bell gave a faint tinkle as though it were made of tin and not of copper.
The little flats in such houses always have bells that ring like that.
He had forgotten the note of that bell, and now its peculiar tinkle seemed to remind him of something and to bring it clearly before him....
He started, his nerves were terribly overstrained by now.
In a little while, the door was opened a tiny crack:
the old woman eyed her visitor with evident distrust through the crack, and nothing could be seen but her little eyes, glittering in the darkness.
But, seeing a number of people on the landing, she grew bolder, and opened the door wide.
The young man stepped into the dark entry, which was partitioned off from the tiny kitchen.
The old woman stood facing him in silence and looking inquiringly at him.
She was a diminutive, withered up old woman of sixty, with sharp malignant eyes and a sharp little nose.
Her colourless, somewhat grizzled hair was thickly smeared with oil, and she wore no kerchief over it.
Round her thin long neck, which looked like a hen’s leg, was knotted some sort of flannel rag, and, in spite of the heat, there hung flapping on her shoulders, a mangy fur cape, yellow with age.
The old woman coughed and groaned at every instant.
The young man must have looked at her with a rather peculiar expression, for a gleam of mistrust came into her eyes again.
M: "If I'm this scared now, what would it be like if I were actually going to do it?"
he couldn't help thinking as he reached the fourth floor.
Some movers blocked his way, carrying furniture out of an apartment.
He knew a German civil servant and his family had lived there.
So this German was moving out, which meant the fourth floor on this staircase would be empty except for the old woman.
"That's a good thing, at least," he thought as he rang the bell of the old woman's apartment.
The bell made a faint tinkling sound, as if it were tin rather than copper.
The small apartments in buildings like these always have bells that sound like that.
He had forgotten the sound of this bell, and now its peculiar tinkling seemed to remind him of something, bringing it sharply into focus....
He flinched -- his nerves were completely shot by now.
After a moment, the door opened a crack.
The old woman peered at her visitor through the gap with obvious suspicion, and nothing was visible but her small eyes, glinting in the darkness.
But when she saw other people on the landing, she grew bolder and opened the door wide.
The young man stepped into the dark entryway, which was separated from the tiny kitchen by a partition.
The old woman stood before him in silence, studying him with a questioning look.
She was a tiny, shriveled woman of about sixty, with sharp, hostile eyes and a sharp little nose.
Her colorless, somewhat graying hair was heavily greased with oil, and she wore nothing on her head.
Around her thin, long neck -- which looked like a chicken's leg -- she had a flannel rag knotted, and despite the heat, a moth-eaten fur cape, yellowed with age, hung loosely from her shoulders.
The old woman coughed and groaned constantly.
The young man must have looked at her with an unusual expression, because a flash of suspicion returned to her eyes.

O: “Now let me tell you my story,” he began, “I came to you, you were asleep.
Then we had dinner and then I went to Porfiry’s, Zametov was still with him.
I tried to begin, but it was no use.
I couldn’t speak in the right way.
They don’t seem to understand and can’t understand, but are not a bit ashamed.
I drew Porfiry to the window, and began talking to him, but it was still no use.
He looked away and I looked away.
At last I shook my fist in his ugly face, and told him as a cousin I’d brain him.
He merely looked at me, I cursed and came away.
That was all.
It was very stupid.
To Zametov I didn’t say a word.
But, you see, I thought I’d made a mess of it, but as I went downstairs a brilliant idea struck me:
why should we trouble?
Of course if you were in any danger or anything, but why need you care?
You needn’t care a hang for them.
We shall have a laugh at them afterwards, and if I were in your place I’d mystify them more than ever.
How ashamed they’ll be afterwards!
Hang them!
We can thrash them afterwards, but let’s laugh at them now!”
M: "Now let me tell you my story," he began.
"I came to you—you were asleep.
Then we had dinner, and I went to Porfiry's.
Zametov was still there.
I tried to get started but couldn't find the right approach.
They don't seem to understand and can't understand, but they're not the least bit embarrassed.
I took Porfiry aside by the window and tried to talk, but it was still hopeless.
He looked away and I looked away.
Finally I shook my fist in his ugly face and told him that as his relative I'd smash his skull.
He just stared at me.
I cursed and left.
That was all.
Very stupid.
To Zametov I said nothing.
But you see, I thought I'd made a mess of it.
Then on the way downstairs a brilliant idea hit me:
why should we care?
If you were in any danger, that would be different.
But why should you care a fig?
You're not connected to any of it.
We'll have a laugh at them later.
If I were you, I'd baffle them even more.
How ashamed they'll be afterward!
Hang them!
We can give them a thrashing later, but for now let's just laugh at them!"

O: The second argument, is from the nature of Monarchy;
wherein all Authority is in one Man, and in others by derivation from him:
But the Government of the Church, he says, is Monarchicall.
This also makes for Christian Monarchs.
For they are really Monarchs of their own people;
that is, of their own Church (for the Church is the same thing with a Christian people;)
whereas the Power of the Pope, though hee were S. Peter, is neither Monarchy, nor hath any thing of Archicall, nor Craticall, but onely of Didacticall;
For God accepteth not a forced, but a willing obedience.
M: The second argument is from the nature of monarchy, in which all authority is in one man, and in others by derivation from him.
But the government of the church, he says, is monarchical.
This also makes for Christian monarchs.

For they are really monarchs of their own people — that is, of their own church (for the church is the same thing as a Christian people) — whereas the power of the pope, even if he were St Peter, is neither monarchy, nor has anything of the archical, nor of the cratical, but only of the didactical.
For God accepts not a forced, but a willing, obedience.

O: But what Commandements are those that God hath given us?
Are all those Laws which were given to the Jews by the hand of Moses, the Commandements of God?
If they bee, why are not Christians taught to obey them?
If they be not, what others are so, besides the Law of Nature?
For our Saviour Christ hath not given us new Laws, but Counsell to observe those wee are subject to;
that is to say, the Laws of Nature, and the Laws of our severall Soveraigns:
Nor did he make any new Law to the Jews in his Sermon on the Mount, but onely expounded the Laws of Moses, to which they were subject before.

The Laws of God therefore are none but the Laws of Nature, whereof the principall is, that we should not violate our Faith, that is, a commandement to obey our Civill Soveraigns, which wee constituted over us, by mutuall pact one with another.

And this Law of God, that commandeth Obedience to the Law Civill, commandeth by consequence Obedience to all the Precepts of the Bible, which (as I have proved in the precedent Chapter) is there onely Law, where the Civill Soveraign hath made it so;
and in other places but Counsell;
which a man at his own perill, may without injustice refuse to obey.
M: But what commandments are those that God has given us?
Are all those laws which were given to the Jews by the hand of Moses the commandments of God?
If they are, why are not Christians taught to obey them?
If they are not, what other laws are so, besides the law of nature?
For our Saviour Christ has not given us new laws, but counsel to observe those we are subject to — that is, the laws of nature, and the laws of our several sovereigns.
Nor did he make any new law to the Jews in his sermon on the mount, but only expounded the laws of Moses, to which they were subject before.

The laws of God therefore are none but the laws of nature, of which the principal is that we should not violate our faith — that is, a commandment to obey our civil sovereigns, whom we constituted over us by mutual pact one with another.
And this law of God, that commands obedience to the civil law, commands by consequence obedience to all the precepts of the Bible;

which (as I have proved in the previous chapter) is there only law, where the civil sovereign has made it so, and in other places is but counsel, which a man, at his own peril, may without injustice refuse to obey.

O: Halesus came, fierce with desire of blood;
But first collected in his arms he stood:
Advancing then, he plied the spear so well, Ladon, Demodocus, and Pheres fell.
Around his head he toss’d his glitt’ring brand, And from Strymonius hew’d his better hand, Held up to guard his throat;
then hurl’d a stone At Thoas’ ample front, and pierc’d the bone:
It struck beneath the space of either eye;
And blood, and mingled brains, together fly.
Deep skill’d in future fates, Halesus’ sire Did with the youth to lonely groves retire:
But, when the father’s mortal race was run, Dire destiny laid hold upon the son, And haul’d him to the war, to find, beneath Th’ Evandrian spear, a memorable death.
Pallas th’ encounter seeks, but, ere he throws, To Tuscan Tiber thus address’d his vows:
“O sacred stream, direct my flying dart, And give to pass the proud Halesus’ heart!
His arms and spoils thy holy oak shall bear.”
Pleas’d with the bribe, the god receiv’d his pray’r:
For, while his shield protects a friend distress’d, The dart came driving on, and pierc’d his breast.
M: Halesus came, fierce with desire of blood;
but first he stood collected in his arms:
advancing then, he plied the spear so well that Ladon, Demodocus, and Pheres fell.
He tossed his glittering brand around his head, and from Strymonius hewed his better hand, held up to guard his throat;
then he hurled a stone at Thoas' ample front, and pierced the bone:
it struck beneath the space of either eye;
and blood, and mingled brains, together flew.
Deeply skilled in future fates, Halesus' sire had retired with the youth to lonely groves;
but, when the father's mortal race was run, dire destiny laid hold upon the son, and hauled him to the war, to find, beneath the Evandrian spear, a memorable death.
Pallas seeks the encounter, but, before he throws, he addresses his vows to Tuscan Tiber thus:
"O sacred stream, direct my flying dart, and grant me to pass through proud Halesus' heart!
Your holy oak shall bear his arms and spoils."
Pleased with the bribe, the god received his prayer:
for, while Halesus' shield protects a distressed friend, the dart came driving on, and pierced his breast.

O: “Ah me!”
she cries, “in this unequal strife What can thy sister more to save thy life?
Weak as I am, can I, alas!
contend In arms with that inexorable fiend?
Now, now, I quit the field!
forbear to fright My tender soul, ye baleful birds of night;
The lashing of your wings I know too well, The sounding flight, and fun’ral screams of hell!
These are the gifts you bring from haughty Jove, The worthy recompense of ravish’d love!
Did he for this exempt my life from fate?
O hard conditions of immortal state, Tho’ born to death, not privileg’d to die, But forc’d to bear impos’d eternity!
Take back your envious bribes, and let me go Companion to my brother’s ghost below!
The joys are vanish’d:
nothing now remains, Of life immortal, but immortal pains.
What earth will open her devouring womb, To rest a weary goddess in the tomb!”
She drew a length of sighs;
nor more she said, But in her azure mantle wrapp’d her head, Then plung’d into her stream, with deep despair, And her last sobs came bubbling up in air.
M: “Ah me!”
she cried.
“In this unequal strife what more can your sister do to save your life?
Weak as I am, can I contend in arms with that inexorable fiend?
Now, now I leave the field!
Forbear to frighten my tender soul, you baleful birds of night!
The lashing of your wings I know too well, the sounding flight, the funeral screams of hell!
These are the gifts you bring from haughty Jove — the worthy recompense of ravished love!
Did he for this exempt my life from fate?
O hard conditions of immortal state — though born to death, not permitted to die, but forced to bear imposed eternity!
Take back your envious gifts, and let me go to be companion to my brother's ghost below!
The joys have vanished;
nothing now remains of immortal life but immortal pain.
What earth will open her devouring womb, to rest a weary goddess in the tomb?”
She drew a long sigh;
she said no more, but wrapped her head in her azure mantle, and plunged into her stream in deep despair, and her last sobs came bubbling up into the air.
